2020-3-s27:
Read the table by pairs of vials. Every patient is in exactly one vial from each pair A/B, C/D, E/F and G/H: patients 1–4 have B and D, 5–8 have B and C, 9–12 have A and D, 13–16 have A and C, and the E/F and G/H choices run FH, FG, EH, EG within each group of four.

So each patient is like a 4-digit binary code, and 16 patients means 16 distinct codes. With exactly one sick patient, exactly one vial in each pair tests positive. That gives the working rules:

  • One of A/B is positive, one of C/D, one of E/F, one of G/H.
  • A negative vial fixes its partner as positive, so the patient is found as soon as one vial in each pair is known.
  • A combination that makes both vials of a pair positive or both negative is impossible.

Patient lookup: pick the vial from each pair, then read off the patient from the table. For the mixing question, a mixed sample goes into the union of the two patients' vials, so the positive count depends on who is actually sick.

Two different patients differ in 1 to 4 of the four pairs, so their union covers 5 to 8 vials. If the sick patient is one of the two mixed ones, the positives number 5, 6, 7 or 8 depending on how many pairs they differ in. If the sick patient is someone else, only that patient's own 4 vials test positive, giving 4.

The possible counts are {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. So the answer is C.

2020-3-s41:
Each round's points add up to a fixed total: all Hi gives −4 in total, all Lo gives +4, and any 1-, 2- or 3-Hi round totals 0. After three rounds the total is 6 − 2 − 2 + 2 = 4, so exactly one of the first three rounds was all Lo and none was all Hi. After six rounds the total is 7 − 1 − 5 − 1 = 0, so the last three rounds hold exactly one all-Hi round (and no all-Lo).

Dipak's third-round score is between his second and first. If round 1 were all Lo, Dipak would have 1 there, so rounds 2 and 3 would need to add to 1 with round 2 below round 3 below 1, which cannot happen. If round 2 were all Lo, round 3 ≥ 2 and round 1 ≥ 3 make his total at least 6. So round 3 is all Lo (+1 for Dipak), with round 1 > 1 and round 2 < 1. Round 1 then gives Dipak 2 (a two-Hi round) and round 2 gives −1. Arun's 6 = 1 + 2 + 3, so he was Hi in round 1 with Dipak (Hi, Lo, Lo, Hi) and the only Hi in round 2 (Hi, Lo, Lo, Lo). Check: Bankim and Charu get −2 − 1 + 1 = −2.

Last three rounds change the scores by +1, +1, −3, −3. One round is all Hi (−1 each), one is Arun alone Hi (the second solo, +3 for Arun, −1 others). The leftover must give Arun −1, Bankim +3, Charu and Dipak −1: Bankim alone Hi. So rounds 4 to 6 are all-Hi, Arun-alone and Bankim-alone in some order.
